title: As days get shorter, TxDOT and Laredo officials urge drivers to watch for pedestrians
excerpt: October and November are the most dangerous months for pedestrians in Texas — 694 people were killed while walking in 2025, and 68% of pedestrian deaths and serious injuries happened after dark.
content:
With daylight fading earlier each evening, TxDOT and Laredo officials are reminding drivers and pedestrians to stay alert — because the months ahead are historically the most dangerous of the year for people on foot, according to KGNS.

In 2025, 694 people were killed by vehicles in Texas while walking, and nearly 20 percent of those deaths happened in October and November, the months with the highest number of crashes involving pedestrians all year, according to the Texas Department of Transportation. Most of those crashes happened at night: 68 percent of pedestrian fatalities and serious injuries in the state last year occurred in the dark.

The risk grows as the days shorten, especially now that daylight saving time has ended. "People walking are already at greater risk when they are near traffic," TxDOT Executive Director Marc Williams said. "But when you add low visibility at night, that risk increases. Drivers and pedestrians alike need to stay alert, visible and focused."

TxDOT is asking drivers to stay alert and scan for pedestrians everywhere, at all times; to stop and yield to pedestrians in crosswalks; to yield the right of way when turning; and to put away their phones. For pedestrians, the agency recommends crossing only at intersections and crosswalks, making eye contact with drivers before crossing, following traffic and crosswalk signals, looking left, right and then left again, putting away phones and earbuds, and wearing reflective materials or carrying a flashlight when it is dark.

Through October and November, TxDOT is also sending out street teams of walking billboards displaying pedestrian safety tips in places across the state where drivers and pedestrians share the road, as part of its "Be Safe. Drive Smart." campaign under the "Drive like a Texan: Kind. Courteous. Safe." initiative.

Sources: KGNS (kgns.tv); Texas Department of Transportation (txdot.gov).
